Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\operatorname{spec}(H)$ is finite and the projections $P_E$ are well-defined, pairwise orthogonal, and sum to $I_d$. Therefore $\Omega_H$ is finite and symmetric, and each $S_a(\omega)$ is a finite sum of endomorphisms of $\mathcal H$; when $m=0$ or a frequency block is empty, the corresponding sum is the zero matrix.

Every term in the displayed formula is a product and finite sum of matrices on $\mathcal H$, so $\mathcal L$ is a complex-linear endomorphism of $M_d(\mathbb C)$. The Hamiltonian coefficient has units joules/(joule-seconds) = seconds$^{-1}$; each dissipative term has units $\gamma_{ab}=\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ times dimensionless matrices. Thus the formula is a well-defined finite linear map with the stated units.

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product. Let $H=H^*$ on $\mathcal H$ be a Hamiltonian matrix with entries in joules, let $\hbar>0$ have units joule-seconds, and let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be a finite family of dimensionless Hermitian matrices, where $m\geq0$. Write the finite spectral decomposition $H=\sum_{E\in\operatorname{spec}(H)} E P_E$, where $P_E$ are pairwise orthogonal spectral projections and $\sum_E P_E=I_d$. The Bohr-frequency set is

$$\Omega_H:=\{(E'-E)/\hbar:E,E'\in\operatorname{spec}(H)\}\subset\mathbb R,$$

whose frequencies have units seconds$^{-1}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega_H$ and $1\leq a\leq m$, define the dimensionless energy-resolved coupling

$$S_a(\omega):=\sum_{\substack{E,E'\in\operatorname{spec}(H)\\E'-E=\hbar\omega}}P_E S_a P_{E'}.$$

Let $\beta\in\mathbb R$ have units joules$^{-1}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega_H$, choose a finite rate matrix $\Gamma(\omega)=(\gamma_{ab}(\omega))_{a,b=1}^m$, with entries in seconds$^{-1}$, that is positive semidefinite in the explicit sense that $\Gamma(\omega)=\Gamma(\omega)^*$ and $v^*\Gamma(\omega)v\geq0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^m$, and require the thermal balance relation

$$\gamma_{ab}(-\omega)=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}\gamma_{ba}(\omega).$$

Let $H_{\rm LS}=H_{\rm LS}^*$ be a Hermitian matrix with units joules satisfying $[H_{\rm LS},H]=0$. For dimensionless $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the finite energy-resolved generator is the linear map

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H+H_{\rm LS},X]+\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_H}\sum_{a,b=1}^{m}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)\left(S_b(\omega)X S_a(\omega)^*-\frac12\{S_a(\omega)^*S_b(\omega),X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. The finite sums define a linear map with units seconds$^{-1}$. This is an adopted finite effective model specification; the definition asserts no microscopic weak-coupling convergence or physical applicability.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a bounded operator $A$ on a complex Banach space, write $e^{tA}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nA^n/n!$ for the operator-norm convergent series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

derivations.claim: For each $\omega$, positive semidefiniteness of the finite matrix $\Gamma(\omega)$ gives a finite factorization $\gamma_{ab}(\omega)=\sum_r\overline{c_{ra}(\omega)}c_{rb}(\omega)$, with $c_{ra}(\omega)$ in seconds$^{-1/2}$. Define $J_{r,\omega}:=\sum_b c_{rb}(\omega)S_b(\omega)$. Expanding yields $\sum_rJ_{r,\omega}XJ_{r,\omega}^*=\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)S_b(\omega)XS_a(\omega)^*$ and $\sum_rJ_{r,\omega}^*J_{r,\omega}=\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)S_a(\omega)^*S_b(\omega)$. Thus the displayed generator has the finite GKSL form of [F2] with Hamiltonian $H+H_{\rm LS}$ and finite jumps $J_{r,\omega}$, so [F3] gives a finite channel semigroup; [F1] states its complete-positivity and trace-preservation content.

From the spectral definition, $[H,S_a(\omega)]=-\hbar\omega S_a(\omega)$ and $S_a(\omega)^*=S_a(-\omega)$. Therefore $S_a(\omega)e^{-\beta H}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}e^{-\beta H}S_a(\omega)$. Every $S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega)$ commutes with $H$ because its two energy shifts cancel, hence it commutes with each spectral projection of $H$ and with $\sigma_\beta$. Also $[H_{\rm LS},H]=0$ implies $H_{\rm LS}$ preserves every eigenspace of $H$: if $Hx=Ex$, then $H(H_{\rm LS}x)=H_{\rm LS}(Hx)=E(H_{\rm LS}x)$. Thus $H_{\rm LS}$ commutes with every spectral projection of $H$ and with $\sigma_\beta$. Finally, the exponential $e^{-\beta H}$ is positive definite with positive finite trace, making $\sigma_\beta$ a faithful density.

Fix $\omega>0$ and put $q=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega}$. The $\omega$ contribution is $\mathcal D_{\omega}(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)(qS_b(\omega)S_a(-\omega)-S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega))$, using $S_b(\omega)\sigma_\beta=q\sigma_\beta S_b(\omega)$ and commutation of the anticommutator product with $\sigma_\beta$. For the negative frequency, substitute $\gamma_{ab}(-\omega)=q\gamma_{ba}(\omega)$ and $S_a(-\omega)^*=S_a(\omega)$, then reindex $a,b$ to obtain $\mathcal D_{-\omega}(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(\omega)(S_a(-\omega)S_b(\omega)-qS_b(\omega)S_a(-\omega))=-\mathcal D_{\omega}(\sigma_\beta)$. Thus every nonzero frequency pair cancels.

At $\omega=0$, the balance relation gives $\gamma_{ab}(0)=\gamma_{ba}(0)$. Each $S_a(0)$ is Hermitian and commutes with $H$, hence with $\sigma_\beta$; consequently the zero-frequency contribution is $\sigma_\beta\sum_{a,b}\gamma_{ab}(0)(S_b(0)S_a(0)-S_a(0)S_b(0))=0$, after swapping $a,b$ in the first finite sum. The Hamiltonian contribution vanishes because both $H$ and $H_{\rm LS}$ commute with $\sigma_\beta$. Together with step 2.1 this gives $\mathcal L(\sigma_\beta)=0$, and the exponential series then gives $T_t(\sigma_\beta)=\sigma_\beta$ for all $t\geq0$.

Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\rho_{ABC}$ be a density operator on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$. With dimensionless entropy $S$ and conditional mutual information $I(A:C\mid B)$ defined by the conventions below,

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC})\ge0.$$

Also let $d,e\ge1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite completely positive trace-preserving map. For all positive semidefinite $X,Y\in M_d(\mathbb C)$,

$$D(\Phi(X)\|\Phi(Y))\le D(X\|Y),$$

where $D$ is the support-sensitive finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy: it equals $\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$ when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, and $+\infty$ otherwise. These are finite-dimensional mathematical statements. The channel inequality is one-sided and asserts no equality condition, recovery map, or infinite-dimensional extension.

$E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$

derivations.claim: On $M_d(\mathbb C)$ use the max-entry norm $\|X\|_{\max}:=\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|$. The space is finite-dimensional and Banach by [F3]. In coordinates, $(\mathcal L X)_{ij}=\sum_{k,l}a_{ij,kl}X_{kl}$ for finitely many coefficients, so $\|\mathcal L X\|_{\max}\leq C\|X\|_{\max}$ with $C:=\max_{i,j}\sum_{k,l}|a_{ij,kl}|<\infty$; thus $\mathcal L$ is bounded. Hence [F4] gives operator-norm convergence of the exponential series, its compact-uniform convergence, and the law $T_uT_v=T_{u+v}$. For $0\leq s\leq t$, put $u=t-s$ and $v=s$. The map $T_{t-s}$ is a finite channel by the hypothesis and [F1], and fixes $\sigma$ by stationarity. Apply [A1] to $X=T_s\rho$ and $Y=\sigma$; these are positive semidefinite, so $D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)\leq D(T_s\rho\|\sigma)$. This proves global monotonicity, including singular initial densities, because $\sigma>0$ makes every displayed relative entropy finite.

For $x>0$ and $R>0$, direct integration gives $\int_0^R((1+s)^{-1}-(x+s)^{-1})\,ds=\log x+\log(1+R)-\log(x+R)$, which tends to $\log x$ as $R\to\infty$. Applying this scalar identity to each eigenvalue using [F2] yields $\log A=\int_0^\infty((1+s)^{-1}I-(A+sI)^{-1})\,ds$ for positive definite $A$. Let $u\mapsto A(u)$ be a $C^1$ path of positive-definite matrices on an open interval, or on a one-sided interval at an endpoint, around the parameter under consideration, and write $X=\dot A(u)$. Differentiating $(A+sI)(A+sI)^{-1}=I$ gives $\frac{d}{du}(A+sI)^{-1}=-(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1}$, so $\frac{d}{du}\log A=\int_0^\infty(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1}\,ds$. At a fixed parameter $u_0$, let $\lambda_0>0$ be the least eigenvalue of $A(u_0)$. By continuity, on a neighborhood $\|A(u)-A(u_0)\|<\lambda_0/2$, so $A(u)\geq(\lambda_0/2)I$ there; since $A'$ is locally bounded, the derivative integrand is uniformly bounded by $C(\lambda_0/2+s)^{-2}$ nearby for some finite $C$, an integrable function. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{du}\operatorname{Tr}(A\log A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log A)+\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Tr}(A(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1})\,ds$. Diagonalize $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j>0$; the integral is $\sum_j X_{jj}\int_0^\infty\lambda_j(\lambda_j+s)^{-2}\,ds=\sum_jX_{jj}=\operatorname{Tr}X$. Hence $\frac{d}{du}\operatorname{Tr}(A\log A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X(\log A+I))$.

For $f(t):=D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)$, every quotient $(f(t+h)-f(t))/h$ with $h>0$ is nonpositive by step 1.1. Thus $D^+f(t):=\limsup_{h\downarrow0}(f(t+h)-f(t))/h\leq0$ as an extended-real upper right Dini derivative, without inserting $\log\rho_t$ when $\rho_t$ is singular.

If $\rho_t>0$, continuity gives a positive-definite neighborhood (right-sided at $t=0$). By [F4], $T_t$ is differentiable in operator norm and $\dot\rho_t=\mathcal L(\rho_t)$. Trace preservation implies $\operatorname{Tr}\dot\rho_t=0$, by differentiating $\operatorname{Tr}(T_t\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho$. Apply step 1.2 to $A=\rho_t$ and differentiate the linear term $-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_t\log\sigma)$ to obtain the displayed derivative formula. Its sign is nonpositive because the same function is nonincreasing by step 1.1.

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\mathcal L:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Define $T_t:=e^{t\mathcal L}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^n\mathcal L^n/n!$ for $t\geq0$, and assume that each $T_t$ is completely positive and trace-preserving; the exponential gives $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$. Let $\sigma=\sigma^*>0$ satisfy $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$ and $T_t(\sigma)=\sigma$ for every $t\geq0$. A density matrix $\rho$ means $\rho=\rho^*$, $v^*\rho v\geq0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^d$, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. For such a density matrix $\rho$, define the finite quantum relative entropy

$$D(\rho\|\sigma):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),$$

using the natural logarithm, the finite spectral logarithm on the support of $\rho$, and $0\log0:=0$. Since $\sigma$ is positive definite, $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ is finite for every density $\rho$. Then $t\mapsto D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)$ is nonincreasing on $[0,\infty)$. If $t$ is interpreted as seconds, $\mathcal L$ has units seconds$^{-1}$; the statement is mathematical and asserts no physical applicability. At every $t\geq0$ for which $\rho_t:=T_t\rho$ is positive definite, its derivative exists (as a right derivative at $t=0$) and

$$\frac{d}{dt}D(\rho_t\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\mathcal L(\rho_t)(\log\rho_t-\log\sigma)\right)\leq0.$$

At singular $\rho_t$ this logarithmic derivative is not asserted; the extended-real upper right Dini derivative is at most zero. No detailed-balance assumption, strict decay, unique stationary state, or convergence to $\sigma$ is asserted.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a bounded operator $A$ on a complex Banach space, write $e^{tA}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nA^n/n!$ for the operator-norm convergent series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.
Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm

derivations.claim: Let $J=\sqrt{\gamma}Z$, which is Hermitian and has units seconds$^{-1/2}$, so $J^*J=\gamma I_2$. Substitution of $H=0$ and this jump into [F2] gives $J\rho J^*-\frac12\{J^*J,\rho\}=\gamma(Z\rho Z-\rho)=\mathcal L(\rho)$. Use the max-entry norm on $M_2(\mathbb C)$; the space is finite-dimensional and hence Banach by [F4]. Since $Z$ is diagonal with entries $1,-1$, $\|\mathcal L(X)\|_{\max}\leq2\gamma\|X\|_{\max}$, so $\mathcal L$ is bounded. Thus [F5] supplies the norm-convergent exponential series. By [F3] and [F1], this generator produces a finite channel semigroup.

Since $H=0$, $e^{-\beta H}=I_2$ and $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}I_2=2$, so the faithful Gibbs density is $\sigma_\beta=I_2/2>0$. Direct multiplication gives $\mathcal L(E_{00})=\mathcal L(E_{11})=0$ and $\mathcal L(E_{01})=-2\gamma E_{01}$, $\mathcal L(E_{10})=-2\gamma E_{10}$. Since $\rho(0)=pE_{00}+(1-p)E_{11}+zE_{01}+\overline zE_{10}$, applying the exponential series [F5] to these four eigenmatrices yields $T_t\rho(0)=pE_{00}+(1-p)E_{11}+e^{-2\gamma t}zE_{01}+e^{-2\gamma t}\overline zE_{10}=\begin{pmatrix}p&e^{-2\gamma t}z\\e^{-2\gamma t}\overline z&1-p\end{pmatrix}$. Every diagonal density is therefore stationary, including the faithful Gibbs density $I_2/2$ and the distinct density $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$.

The hypotheses of [A1] hold by steps 1.1 and 1.2, so relative entropy to $I_2/2$ is nonincreasing in this example. Yet $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ remains fixed and differs from $I_2/2$ for every $t\geq0$. Hence the Gibbs density is not the unique stationary density, and this initial state does not converge to it, refuting both conclusions.
